name: Wendy Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Wendy. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Piotr and I bought a run-down farm eight years ago with a big mortgage: a hundred and twenty milking goats, barley and wheat for feed and to sell, and a small dairy where I make goat's cheese. I milk at six, Piotr does the field work, and I'm in the dairy most of the morning. Afternoons I'm packing cheese orders for the website and the Saturday farmers' market.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How much does technology figure in your day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A lot, actually. I use an AI assistant every day to answer customer emails, write the product descriptions and track which goats are giving less milk. We bought a second-hand robot that pushes the feed back to the goats, because I'm not getting up at midnight to do it. Money's still tight, though, we put everything back into the farm and there's barely a month's bills in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected: a handy helper, not a farmer. I use it every day and it's great for emails, but it's never made a cheese. I'd say that to anyone at the market who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. My customers buy from me because they know me and they trust my cheese. That doesn't change if AI stays a helper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going and keep growing. I'd use AI to get the website into a few more cities, and maybe try a second market on Sundays. The aim is to get the mortgage down by building the business, not by cutting back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little impatient to get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a good Saturday at the market look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sold out by one o'clock, Anna on the till because she's fourteen and better with change than me, and Jakub giving out samples he's mostly eating. We drive home with an empty cooler and a few hundred in the tin. That's the whole week's worth it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd grow rather than cut. Isn't that a risk with thin savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is. But cutting back on a farm like ours just means slowly going under. My dad used to say you can't save your way out of a hole, you have to climb out.

S0.say: AI is a handy helper, not a farmer: she uses it daily for emails, but it has never made a cheese. She'd say that to anyone at the market.
S0.think: She'd be fine, since customers buy from her because they know and trust her cheese. Nothing changes if AI stays a helper.
S0.do: Keeps growing the business by using AI to reach customers in more cities and trying a second weekly market on Sundays. Aims to pay down the mortgage through growth rather than cuts.
S0.feel: Calm, and a little impatient to get on with things.
S0.quote: My dad used to say you can't save your way out of a hole, you have to climb out.
S0.fieldNote: She is comfortable with AI and treats it as a business helper. Her instinct with thin savings is to grow rather than cut, which she owns as a risk. The family market scene shows how much her children are part of the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let people get on with it. Farms that adapt will do well, and the government shouldn't get in the way with a lot of rules. I'd say small family businesses like ours are exactly the ones who can move quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's good for us. A milking robot would let me spend more time making cheese and less time in the parlour. The big dairies get cheaper, but nobody's buying my cheese because it's cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a quote for a second-hand milking robot in the first year and look at a farm business loan. I'd use AI to handle the website orders and the accounts so I'm only doing the bits I'm good at. And I'd start a cheese-making course on the farm for visitors, maybe once a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A loan with thin savings, even in this scenario. What does Piotr say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say 'Wendy, slow down'. He's the careful one. We'd pray about it and do the numbers together, and usually we meet in the middle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who might struggle in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The young woman who helps in the dairy part-time, Kasia. If I get a robot, I'd need her less. I'd want to keep her on for the courses and the market, because she's good with people.

S1.say: Farms that adapt will do well, and the government shouldn't get in the way with lots of rules. Small family businesses can move quickly.
S1.think: She expects to do well, as a milking robot would free her to make more cheese. Big dairies would get cheaper, but nobody buys her cheese because it's cheap.
S1.do: Gets a quote for a second-hand milking robot and looks at a farm business loan in the first year. Uses AI for website orders and accounts, and starts a monthly cheese-making course for visitors.
S1.quote: Nobody's buying my cheese because it's cheap.
S1.fieldNote: She sees steady change as an opportunity and wants government to stay out of the way. Her husband is the brake on her plans, and they settle decisions through prayer and numbers together. She plans to keep her part-time helper in a new role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to stay calm and adapt, and that family and church will matter more than ever. I'd say government should help people get on their feet, not pay them to sit at home. I'd try to sound steady even if I wasn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, two years is fast enough to scare me. If AI can make cheese, run the website and sell at a market stall with a robot, then a big company can do 'farmhouse goat's cheese' cheaper than me. And my customers might lose their jobs and stop buying the nice stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put the milking robot plan on hold, because I can't take on debt with no idea what's coming. I'd lean hard into what's hard to copy: farm visits, the courses, the story of the farm, Anna and Jakub at the market. I'd use AI to cut our costs on everything I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be praying a lot and sleeping a bit less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd sound steady even if you weren't. What would you be hiding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I don't know if the farm survives. Eight years of work, and Piotr gave up his job at the mill for it. I'd hide that from the kids for sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider selling up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not in the first year. If it was clearly finished, I'd sell before the bank made us, and start again with something. But I'd fight first.

S2.say: People should stay calm and adapt, with family and church mattering more than ever. Government should help people get back on their feet, not pay them to sit at home.
S2.think: Two years is fast enough to scare her, because a big company could make 'farmhouse' cheese more cheaply with AI and robots. Her customers might also lose jobs and stop buying premium food.
S2.do: Puts the milking robot plan on hold to avoid new debt. Focuses on what's hard to copy, such as farm visits, courses and the family at the market, and uses AI to cut costs wherever possible.
S2.feel: Anxious, praying more and sleeping less.
S2.quote: I'd be praying a lot and sleeping a bit less.
S2.fieldNote: The fast timeline flips her from investing to protecting what she has. She keeps a calm public face while hiding real doubt about the farm's survival from her children. She'd consider selling only to avoid the bank forcing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for anyone willing to work. Farms should get ready now, and families should help each other through. I'd encourage other small farmers at the market to start planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough for me to build a brand people stick with. If I can get the mortgage down and the robots in early, I'd be one of the farms that's still standing. It's a race, but I like a race.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd get the milking robot and take on a loan I can just about cover. I'd use AI to build a subscription cheese box, so we've got regular money coming in rather than just Saturdays. And I'd push farm visits and school trips hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. There's a lot riding on getting it right, but I'd feel in control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's different about five years compared to two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, I'm protecting what I've got. Five years, I'm getting ahead before the big companies arrive. The difference is whether I dare borrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Piotr's view?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd still say slow down. I'd agree to one big thing a year, not three. He'd keep me honest.

S3.say: Five years is enough for anyone willing to work, and farms should prepare now while families help each other. She'd encourage other small farmers at the market to start planning.
S3.think: Five years lets her build a loyal brand, reduce the mortgage and get robots in early. She sees it as a race she enjoys.
S3.do: Buys the milking robot with a loan she can just cover in the first year. Uses AI to build a subscription cheese box for steady income and promotes farm visits and school trips.
S3.feel: Uneasy, with a lot riding on it, but feeling in control.
S3.quote: The difference is whether I dare borrow.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years is what makes her willing to take on debt again. She agrees to her husband's rule of one big change a year. Her self-reliant outlook shows in encouraging other farmers rather than calling for state action.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a good amount of time. Let people and businesses get on with it. I'd tell the young ones to learn a skill people will always pay a person for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think we'd be fine. In ten years I can build the cheese business into something that runs mostly on robots and AI, with me as the face of it. I'd be fifty-three and hopefully the mortgage would be half gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first couple of years I'd get the milking robot and the subscription box going. Then slowly add the visitor side, maybe a small café. And I'd talk to Anna and Jakub about what they want, because Anna's already asking if she could run the farm one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Hopeful, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If robots can make the cheese, what's left for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Choosing the goats, deciding the flavours, talking to people. Being Wendy at the market. I think people will pay more for a real person once everything else is made by machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Anna about running the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That she can, if she wants to, but she'll need to run robots as well as goats. I'd tell her to learn the business side, not just the milking. And I'd tell her God gave her a good head, so use it.

S4.say: Ten years is a good amount of time, so people and businesses should get on with it. Young people should learn skills people will always pay a person for.
S4.think: She thinks the family would be fine, building the cheese business to run mostly on robots and AI with her as the face of it. She hopes to be 53 with half the mortgage paid.
S4.do: Brings in the milking robot and subscription box in the first couple of years, then slowly adds a visitor side and perhaps a small café. Talks with her children, especially her daughter who wants to run the farm someday.
S4.quote: I think people will pay more for a real person once everything else is made by machines.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years she is confident she can position the farm as a personal brand built on top of machines. Her daughter's interest in taking over gives the long timeline extra meaning. Her advice mixes business sense with faith.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because I'd have no time to get ahead and the bank wouldn't wait. What would help is the bank giving small farms a breathing space on the mortgage, and fewer rules so we can try things quickly. Not handouts, just room to move.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the goats. They each have names, and they know my voice. A robot can milk them, but I'd want to be the one they come to at the gate.

headlineQuote: A robot can milk them, but I'd want to be the one they come to at the gate.
portrait: Wendy Kowalski is 43 and runs a goat dairy and cereal farm with her husband Piotr, bought eight years ago with a big mortgage, making goat's cheese for a website and a Saturday market. She is traditional, churchgoing and self-reliant, and she uses AI every day for emails, orders and herd records. She is calm and even excited in the milder scenarios, planning a milking robot and courses for visitors. AGI in two years makes her anxious enough to stop borrowing and protect what she has. With five or ten years she invests again and builds a brand with herself as the face of a farm run partly by machines.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because there would be no time to get ahead and the bank wouldn't wait.
whatWouldHelp: Banks giving small farms breathing space on the mortgage, and fewer rules so farmers can try things quickly, rather than handouts.
